story: Think summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun? Think again! Our planet actually reaches perihelion—its closest point to the Sun—in early January, during the depths of the Northern Hemisphere's winter. Conversely, we are farthest from the Sun, at aphelion, in early July. This orbital distance variation has almost nothing to do with our seasons. Instead, we have seasons because Earth's axis is tilted at a 23.4-degree angle. As we orbit the Sun, this tilt remains fixed. When a hemisphere leans toward the Sun, it receives more direct, intense sunlight and longer days, sparking summer. When it tilts away, winter arrives with shorter, colder days and indirect light. This means the Northern and Southern hemispheres always experience opposite seasons. At the poles, this tilt creates months of continuous summer daylight or total winter darkness, while the equator stays seasonless year-round.
angle: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January (during winter in the Northern Hemisphere) and farthest from the Sun in July (during summer), proving that orbital distance does not cause the seasons.
disputed: The exact duration of axial precession is given as 26,000 years in S2 but 25,771.5 years in S3. A script should use 'about 26,000 years' to align with both.

The relative importance of precession versus obliquity in driving climate is noted as a matter of ongoing study in S3, while S1 notes the overall impact of orbital forcing remains poorly constrained; the script should avoid presenting either as fully settled.
